parts:
Gaspard, I can’t see the attached image, but I am afraid that you would need to consider each camp as an independent sampling unit.  Whether 8-10 is sufficient replication depends on how heterogeneous density is.  If the environment is relatively homogeneous, that might be fine.  If not, your analysis will still be valid, but confidence intervals may be wide.  You’ll have the advantage of lots of data per camp, so that you should at least have fairly precise data from each camp.

 

You should consider a more model-based approach.  For example you can fit a density surface model using the dsm engine of distance, and hence estimate density through the park by that means.

 

Steve

From: distance...@googlegroups.com [mailto:distance...@googlegroups.com] On Behalf Of gaspard van hamme
Sent: 31 January 2020 10:16
To: distance-sampling <distance...@googlegroups.com>
Subject: [distance-sampling] Cluster sampling design using Point transects

 

Hi all, 

 

I would like to ask your advice concerning cluster sampling. I am novice to distance sampling and was not able to find anything similar to our situation in the design sections of general distance sampling books (Buckland et al. 1993; Strindberg et al. 2004; Buckland et al. 2015) and specialised primate sections (Peres 1999; Buckland et al. 2010; Ross and Reeve 2011).

 

Context

I have the opportunity to join a team currently conducting a bird survey in a forested national park in the Philippines, in order to conduct a separate macaque population survey while benefiting from their logistics. This is in an area where we know little about the primates. However, this situation also means that my survey is restricted by their plan, and I am doubting about the most efficient design to adopt within their conditions. 

 

Planning

·      The survey will be conducted from bivouac camps in the park, during week-long expeditions comprising 2 camps each. 

·      For the location of the camps, they made a grid of 2,5 km-wide squares in the middle of which the camps will be set (see attached). The blue dots represent the camp locations which were randomly chosen, yet I will only be able to access 8-10 of them in the time of the study (4-5 expeditions). The camps visited are still to be confirmed, but chosen indenpendently from the terrain or animal distribution.

·      In each camp we will stay 2 days surveying the grid square. 

 

As As of today, I plan to follow their methodology, i.e. doing point counts every 250m on 1 km transects (2 or 3 per camp) spreading out from the camps (in a cross pattern). Yet, I wonder if this design will allow to draw inferences to estimate reliable density and abundance for the whole park.

 

According to Buckland et al. (2015:16) “If the separation of neighbouring points on the same line is less than the separation of neighbouring points on different lines, then this should be treated as cluster sampling, where each line represents one cluster of points.” 

  • Is there a problem to consider the 2 or more lines of points departing 250m from a same camp (to avoid human disturbance bias and overlapping) as independent sampling units? 
  • Would using this sampling design respect the principles of survey design? 

It seems that considering the different point transects from one camp together as one sampling unit would produce data-rich samples but insufficient in number (8-10) for adequate replication. 

 

Thanks for your help, 

Gaspard

 

Ps: please pardon the lengthy message. The attached grid has been designed due to the absence of a trail system and accidented terrain making travel difficult. The grid covers most of the park's territory which does not reach the coast.
